entities.name: 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, also known as the Great East Japan earthquake, occurred on March 11, 2011, at 2:46 p.m. local time, off the east coast of Japan's main island, Honshu. This massive event was a megathrust earthquake, centered approximately 43 miles east of the Oshika Peninsula, with a magnitude of 9.1, making it one of the largest earthquakes in recorded history. The earthquake's massive tsunami waves devastated the coastal regions of Miyagi, Iwate, and Fukushima prefectures, causing widespread destruction, with over 15,000 people killed and countless more displaced. The disaster also triggered a meltdown at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant, leading to a radioactive contamination of the surrounding area.

The aftermath of the disaster saw a massive relief effort, with rescue teams working tirelessly to reach stranded survivors, and international aid pouring in to support the affected communities. The disaster also led to a significant shift in Japan's energy policy, with a greater emphasis on renewable energy sources and a reduction in reliance on nuclear power.

The 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami had a profound impact on the lives of millions of people, and its effects are still being felt today. The disaster served as a wake-up call for the world, highlighting the importance of disaster preparedness and the need for more effective emergency response systems.

One of the most enduring legacies of the disaster is the continued struggle of many communities to recover and rebuild. As one survivor noted, 'We are still living in the shadow of the tsunami, trying to rebuild our lives and our communities.'
